chapter: Theater broadcasts, recordings and the road
title: Why the New York and New Orleans recordings sound different; studio dubbing
summary: Asked about the band's sound, he says New York used studio men and describes how film studios dub and time music to pictures.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Oh, I wanted to ask you.
Ask me something that you want to know.
Yeah, that I want to know too. Your band sounded different in the New York recording from the New Orleans recording. It is, huh? And I was wondering why.

Maybe they went and got some good New York musicians to put them in there. I didn't know that. They'd feel that all over the world. Don't you know that my brother went to the studios? If you can't hit a high note, they'll have one to hit it for you. If you can't sing the high note, they got somebody who can sing it. They'll dub anything. They'll dub anything. A case of point was that Alfredo and the musicians never see the picture they're recording for. Did you know that?

They wouldn't go see it if you gave them a ticket. They just play the music. And in the drum section, it's done electrically, like the leader. They have earphones because of everything. So they do, they have arranges. Guys say, give me 12 minutes or 12 seconds of a guy falling off a cliff or a horse or something. They jot it down. It'll last again. Nip it off. Join it together. All spells mother. Band never sees the picture. It's all timed.
But your New York recordings had a two-bone. They're too long you say? No, there's a tuba, tuba player.
